FACT_ID: sec05-F01 | anchor: A18
Clear vision helps a driver identify traffic and road conditions, notice hazards and respond promptly. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F02 | anchor: A18
South Dakota requires a vision test before issuing a driver license. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F03 | anchor: A18
An unrestricted license requires vision of at least 20/40 with both eyes and no worse than 20/50 in either eye. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F04 | anchor: A18
Peripheral vision helps detect vehicles or hazards beside the driver, but side mirrors and side glances are still needed because side objects cannot be sharply focused. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F05 | anchor: A18
Judging distance and speed takes practice and matters when choosing gaps for merging, passing on two-lane roads or crossing ahead of a train. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F06 | anchor: A18
A driver with trouble seeing at night should limit unnecessary night driving and take particular care when driving after dark. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F07 | anchor: A18
The handbook advises regular eye examinations because seeing well is important to safe driving. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F08 | anchor: A18
A driver whose license requires corrective lenses must wear them whenever driving and risks a ticket for driving without them. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F09 | anchor: A18
Dark or tinted corrective lenses should be avoided at night because they reduce the light available for seeing. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F10 | anchor: A18
Keeping spare glasses in the vehicle helps when the usual pair is broken, lost or misplaced. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F11 | anchor: A18
Horns, sirens and skidding-tire sounds can warn a driver of danger. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F12 | anchor: A18
A driver who knows of hearing loss can compensate by relying more on vision and staying alert. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F13 | anchor: A18
The handbook reports that hearing-impaired drivers’ driving records are as good as those of drivers with good hearing. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F14 | anchor: A18
Fatigue means physical or mental tiredness and may follow exertion, repetitive tasks, illness or insufficient sleep. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F15 | anchor: A18
Fatigue can impair vision and lengthen decision time, so the handbook advises against driving while tired. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F16 | anchor: A18
Before a trip, the handbook advises enough sleep and notes that most people need 7 to 9 hours for daytime alertness. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F17 | anchor: A18
Trip planning should include a stop about every 100 miles or every 2 hours. [A18]
Source: [A18 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0018]

FACT_ID: sec05-F18 | anchor: A19
A travel companion can help by watching the driver’s driving. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F19 | anchor: A19
Before driving, check medicine labels for drowsiness warnings. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F20 | anchor: A19
The handbook advises against alcohol or drug use when driving. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F21 | anchor: A19
A driver who starts feeling tired should leave the road at the next exit or rest area for a 15-to-20-minute nap or find overnight accommodation. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F22 | anchor: A19
The handbook suggests caffeine before a short nap to combine the two effects. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F23 | anchor: A19
Avoiding late-night driving and getting plenty of rest are the handbook’s fatigue-prevention recommendations. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F24 | anchor: A19
A distraction is anything that shifts attention away from driving, including mental activity even when the eyes and hands do not visibly move. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F25 | anchor: A19
Distracted driving can cause crashes involving injury, death or property damage. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F26 | anchor: A19
State law prohibits texting, reading messages and social networking while driving. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F27 | anchor: A19
Drivers should avoid arguments, emotionally stressful conversations and eating while driving. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F28 | anchor: A19
Children should be safely restrained and pets should be secured in a carrier or portable kennel. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F29 | anchor: A19
Instruction-permit and restricted-permit holders may not use wireless communication devices while operating a motor vehicle. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F30 | anchor: A19
Drivers are responsible for paying attention and operating their vehicle safely. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F31 | anchor: A19
Aggressive driving involves an intentional action that endangers another person or property. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F32 | anchor: A19
Typical aggressive-driving behaviors include speeding, following too closely, unsafe lane changes, faulty signaling and ignoring traffic controls. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F33 | anchor: A19
The handbook advises concentrating on driving and treating other road users patiently and courteously. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F34 | anchor: A19
The handbook estimates that alcohol or other impairing drugs are involved in about 40 percent of fatal traffic crashes each year. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F35 | anchor: A19
Even small amounts of alcohol or other impairing drugs increase crash risk compared with driving without them. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F36 | anchor: A19
Alcohol has a greater effect on new drivers because they are still learning the driving skills. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F37 | anchor: A19
Driving after drinking can bring substantial fines, increased insurance costs, license loss or jail. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F38 | anchor: A19
A person under 21 may not buy, possess or drink alcoholic beverages. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F39 | anchor: A19
Alcohol and other impairing drugs interfere with perceiving surroundings, responding to emergencies and controlling a vehicle skillfully. [A19]
Source: [A19 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0019]

FACT_ID: sec05-F40 | anchor: A20
Physical control of a vehicle can be enough for arrest when BAC exceeds the legal limit, even if the person is not driving. [A20]
Source: [A20 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0020]

FACT_ID: sec05-F41 | anchor: A20
Driving on a public highway gives consent to a chemical test under the handbook’s implied-consent description. [A20]
Source: [A20 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0020]

FACT_ID: sec05-F42 | anchor: A20
The handbook identifies BAC of at least 0.08 percent, or at least 0.02 percent for someone under 21, as evidence of alcohol-impaired driving. [A20]
Source: [A20 -> src:rdmv-sd-l:south-dakota-department-of-public-safety:handbook:pdf-0020]

Misconceptions: Looking sober does not prove safe driving, being below the listed BAC threshold does not rule out impairment, and prescription or over-the-counter status does not establish driving safety.
Mnemonics: Use see, rest, focus and avoid impairment as an authored retrieval cue, without replacing the cited rules.
Glossary: Fatigue is physical or mental tiredness; distraction takes attention from driving; aggressive driving intentionally endangers people or property; BAC describes alcohol concentration relative to blood.
Dynamic facts: Fatal-crash statistics and printed sanctions are snapshot claims requiring current issuer verification. Personal medical eligibility is not certified by this dossier.
